newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage ordeal passes three-month milestone.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage ordeal passes three-month milestone.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis passed its three-month milestone on Monday with prospects still distant for an end to the grueling ordeal for 72 dignitaries held under the gun by Marxist rebels.

Peruvians banged pots, rang church bells and sounded car horns to demand freedom for the men held at the Japanese ambassador's home and mediators shuttled between meetings to unblock stalled talks to find a peaceful end to the crisis.
But in a short speech on the 90th day of the siege, President Alberto Fujimori had little to offer his country beyond lamenting the captives' plight as a "terrible situation."

The three-member guarantors commission first met with Fujimori at Government Palace, then with Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels at a Red Cross safe house across the street from the diplomatic compound. But they made no comments after four hours of meetings.
Earlier, families of the hostages holed up in the mansion staged a day of solidarity, including a noisy nationwide demonstration at midday.
In a chaotic cacophany outside the residence, car owners set off their alarms, neighbours came out to bang pots, pans and bottles, and demonstrators blew whistles and chanted.
In the surrounding San Isidro neighbourhood -- as throughout Peru -- churches held special masses and rang bells in a sign of support for the captives.
In Lima, motorists sounded horns, and legislators came out of Congress to hold a minute's silence in a nearby square before applauding and shouting for the hostages' freedom.
"I hope that inside they all feel that we are with them, that we love them," Beatriz de Gumucio, wife of captive Bolivian ambassador Jorge Gumucio, said outside the residence.

"The whole of Peru has united for this group of 72 dignified people," said Luisa Aguilar, wife of captive judge Hugo Sivina. "I am sure that the terrorists have heard us and realised that there is no room for them in this country. Nobody is with them."
Some of the hostages responded by raising hands to a window sandwiched between a rebel flag and a banner railing against Fujimori. One of them waved a white handkerchief.
An open letter from the families described the time since the MRTA takeover of the diplomatic compound as "three months of agony and suffering."

More than 500 hostages were taken on Dec. 17 when about 20 jungle-trained rebels blew a hole in the residence's outer wall and swarmed into the building in a fierce shootout. But the MRTA gradually released most of its prisoners, keeping those it considered most valuable as bargaining chips to demand the freedom of some 400 jailed comrades.

The remaining captives -- top diplomats, security chiefs, government ministers, judges and businessmen -- are mainly middle-aged and increasingly ailing, intelligence and medical reports say. Stress, gum diseases and skin ailments are common.
The hostages have already passed Christmas and New Year inside the cramped building with the windows closed and no air conditioning. They looked likely to spend Easter there, too.

"The basic problem is now almost the same as 90 days ago -- how to deal with the demand for freedom of MRTA prisoners," former captive and opposition legislator Javier Diez Canseco, released in the early days of the crisis, told Reuters.
"I think of the hostages every day, of what they are going through," he added.

Bolivian Foreign Minister Antonio Aranibar sent a greeting to his ambassador and called for reflection at the three-month milestone. "Ninety days is too much. However, there is no short-term solution in sight," he told local radio in a phone interview from La Paz.
Mediators are seeking to find a negotiated solution after 10 rounds of face-to-face talks brought little more than an exchange of divergent positions.
A leading pollster said more than half of Peruvians believed the crisis -- already Latin America's longest hostage siege -- would take at least one month more to resolve.
